claims.text: The superconducting critical temperature of high-entropy alloys is governed by the degree of configurational disorder.
Increasing configurational disorder increases lattice strain or local lattice distortion.
Increasing configurational disorder increases electron scattering.
Disorder-induced lattice distortion and electron scattering alter the density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level modify electron–phonon coupling.
Electron–phonon coupling drives superconductivity in the proposed alloy.
A high-entropy alloy contains at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
A fully random atomic distribution represents the high- or maximum-configurational-disorder baseline.
Introducing slight compositional clustering reduces configurational disorder.
The random and clustered samples can be compared while retaining the same elemental ratios, single-phase structure, and processing conditions.
Local variations in atomic spacing produce lattice strain.
Reducing disorder through controlled clustering should produce a measurable shift in critical temperature relative to the fully random baseline.
A critical-temperature shift should occur together with detectable changes in electron–phonon coupling strength and density of states.
Tunneling spectroscopy can measure the proposed changes in electron–phonon coupling and density of states.
X-ray diffraction can detect the proposed variation in lattice strain.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase crystalline high-entropy alloys in the low-temperature superconducting regime.
The proposed effect requires changes in local atomic arrangement that affect lattice strain and electronic interactions without causing phase separation.
The direction of the critical-temperature response to disorder may be either positive or negative.
The magnitude and direction of the response depend on the elemental combination and local bonding environment.
A confirmed disorder difference without statistically significant changes in critical temperature, electron–phonon coupling, or density of states would falsify the hypothesis.
